recipes.title: Greek Tzatziki with Cucumber
recipes.blurb: Thick strained yogurt, squeezed cucumber, garlic, and dill — cool, sharp, and ready for anything grilled. The one non-negotiable step is getting the water out of the cucumber.

items: 2 cups (480 g) full-fat Greek yogurt, 5 percent or 10 percent
1 large English cucumber (about 12 oz / 340 g)
1 tsp (6 g) kosher salt, for drawing water out of the cucumber
3 garlic cloves, grated to a paste (about 1 tbsp)
2 tbsp (30 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for drizzling
1 tbsp (15 ml) fresh lemon juice
1 tsp (5 ml) red wine vinegar
2 tbsp (about 5 g) finely chopped fresh dill
1 tbsp finely chopped fresh mint, optional
¾ tsp (4 g) fine sea salt, for the sauce
¼ tsp (0.5 g) freshly ground white pepper

instructions.title: Start with real Greek yogurt
instructions.text: Use full-fat strained Greek yogurt, not regular yogurt and not a low-fat version. Regular yogurt has far too much whey and will turn soupy within an hour no matter how well you drain the cucumber, and low-fat yogurt tastes thin and sour once the garlic goes in. If all you can find is regular yogurt, strain it through cheesecloth in the fridge for 4 hours first.

instructions.title: Grate the cucumber
instructions.text: Trim the ends and grate the whole cucumber on the large holes of a box grater, skin and all — English cucumber skin is thin, tender, and adds flecks of green. Do not peel or seed it if you are using an English or Persian cucumber. If you only have a standard waxy field cucumber, peel it and scrape out the watery seed core with a spoon.

instructions.title: Salt and drain it
instructions.text: Toss the grated cucumber with the 1 tsp kosher salt in a colander set over a bowl and let it sit for 20 to 30 minutes. Salt draws water out of the cells by osmosis, and you will be genuinely surprised how much liquid collects underneath. This step is the entire difference between tzatziki and watery yogurt soup.

instructions.title: Squeeze it bone dry
instructions.text: Gather the drained cucumber in a clean kitchen towel or a few layers of cheesecloth and wring it hard over the sink. Keep twisting until almost nothing more comes out — expect to remove roughly ½ cup (120 ml) of liquid. The cucumber should look compressed and almost dry, and yes, this feels like too much, and yes, it is correct.

instructions.title: Make garlic paste
instructions.text: Grate the 3 garlic cloves on a Microplane, or mince them and then smear them against the cutting board with the side of your knife and a pinch of salt until they form a paste. Chunks of raw garlic in tzatziki are unpleasantly hot in the mouth and only get sharper overnight. A true paste distributes the flavor evenly through the yogurt.

instructions.title: Mellow the garlic in acid
instructions.text: Stir the garlic paste together with the 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp red wine vinegar in a small bowl and let it stand 5 minutes. The acid deactivates some of the allicin, which is the compound responsible for raw garlic's aggressive burn. Skip this and the sauce will be noticeably harsher on day two.

instructions.title: Combine everything
instructions.text: In a medium bowl, stir together the yogurt, squeezed cucumber, garlic-lemon mixture, olive oil, dill, mint if using, ¾ tsp fine sea salt, and white pepper. Fold gently with a spatula rather than beating it — vigorously whisked yogurt breaks down and turns runny. It should look thick enough to hold the mark of the spatula.

instructions.title: Chill for at least an hour
instructions.text: Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or up to overnight. The garlic, dill, and cucumber need time to move into the yogurt, and tzatziki eaten immediately tastes like three separate ingredients in a bowl. It also firms up as it chills, so judge the final texture cold, not warm.

instructions.title: Taste and finish
instructions.text: Taste it cold and adjust — it should be tangy, garlicky, and clearly salted, since it is meant to season whatever it lands on. Add salt ⅛ tsp at a time and another squeeze of lemon if it tastes rich rather than fresh. If it has loosened at all, stir in 2 tbsp (30 g) more yogurt.

instructions.title: Serve it cold
instructions.text: Spread it in a shallow bowl, drag the back of a spoon through it to make a swirl, and pour a little olive oil into the groove with a few dill fronds on top. Serve straight from the fridge at 38°F to 40°F (3°C to 4°C) with warm pita, grilled lamb, chicken souvlaki, or roasted potatoes. It keeps 4 days refrigerated, though the garlic strengthens each day.

tips: Make it a day ahead if you can. Tzatziki is genuinely better on day two, once the garlic has settled into the yogurt.
Watery tzatziki is always a cucumber problem, never a yogurt problem. Squeeze harder than you think you should.
For a Turkish cacik, thin the finished sauce with ¼ cup (60 ml) cold water and serve it as a chilled soup-like dip with extra mint.

It doubles as a salad dressing thinned with a little water, and as a marinade for chicken thighs, which the yogurt's acid and enzymes tenderize beautifully — grill them to 165°F (74°C) and throw the used marinade away.
recipes.keyTemp: No cooking. Serve cold, 38°F to 40°F (3°C to 4°C) — warm tzatziki tastes flat and the raw garlic reads much harsher.
recipes.pairing: Warm pita and grilled lamb or chicken souvlaki; a cold Greek white like Assyrtiko or just an ice-cold beer.

recipes.title: Thai Peanut Dipping Sauce
recipes.blurb: Coconut milk, red curry paste, and peanut butter simmered into something rich, salty, and just sweet enough. Twenty minutes, and it turns satay, noodles, or plain rice into dinner.

items: 1 can (13.5 oz / 400 ml) full-fat coconut milk, unshaken
2 tbsp (32 g) Thai red curry paste
⅔ cup (170 g) natural creamy peanut butter, ideally just peanuts and salt
3 tbsp (45 ml) fish sauce, or soy sauce or tamari to keep it vegetarian
3 tbsp (40 g) palm sugar or packed light brown sugar
2 tbsp (30 ml) fresh lime juice
1 tbsp (15 ml) rice vinegar
1 garlic clove, finely grated (about 1 tsp)
1 tsp (2 g) finely grated fresh ginger
¼ to ½ cup (60 to 120 ml) warm water, for thinning
2 tbsp (18 g) roasted peanuts, roughly chopped, for garnish

instructions.title: Do not shake the coconut milk
instructions.text: Open the can without shaking it and spoon the thick white cream off the top into a saucepan, setting the thinner liquid aside for later. That solid cream is nearly pure coconut fat, and you are going to fry the curry paste in it. This technique is called cracking the coconut cream and it is the step that separates a real Thai peanut sauce from a smoothie.

instructions.title: Crack the coconut cream
instructions.text: Heat the coconut cream in a 2-quart (2 L) saucepan over medium heat for 3 to 5 minutes, stirring occasionally. It will bubble, thicken, and then visibly separate as clear coconut oil pools at the edges — that is exactly what you want. If your coconut milk has stabilizers and refuses to split, just carry on; add 1 tbsp (15 ml) of neutral oil to compensate.

instructions.title: Fry the curry paste
instructions.text: Add the 2 tbsp red curry paste to the hot fat and fry it, mashing and stirring, for 2 to 3 minutes until it darkens a shade and smells intensely aromatic. Frying paste in fat rather than just stirring it into liquid unlocks the chile, lemongrass, and galangal oils that are otherwise locked in. The kitchen should smell like a Thai restaurant at this point.

instructions.title: Add aromatics
instructions.text: Stir in the grated garlic and the 1 tsp grated ginger and cook for just 30 seconds more, keeping everything moving with a wooden spoon. Grated this finely they cook almost instantly, and left any longer in fat this hot they scorch and turn acrid — a bitterness you cannot take back out of the sauce. What you want is for the raw, sharp edge to disappear and the smell to turn sweet and fragrant. If the pan looks dry or the paste starts catching, slide it off the burner for a few seconds rather than adding liquid.

instructions.title: Whisk in the peanut butter
instructions.text: Add the ⅔ cup peanut butter and whisk hard — it will seize into a stiff, alarming paste for a moment, which is completely normal. Keep whisking and add the reserved thin coconut liquid a little at a time, and it will loosen into a smooth sauce over about a minute. Natural peanut butter with no added sugar or hydrogenated oil gives a far cleaner flavor than the sweetened supermarket kind.

instructions.title: Season the sauce
instructions.text: Whisk in the fish sauce, palm sugar, and rice vinegar and stir until the sugar has fully dissolved, about 1 minute. Thai cooking balances salty, sweet, sour, and spicy, and this is the moment you set those four dials. Palm sugar has a caramel note that brown sugar approximates well, so use whichever you can find.

instructions.title: Simmer gently
instructions.text: Let the sauce bubble gently for 3 to 4 minutes at around 190°F (88°C), stirring frequently and scraping the bottom of the pan where the peanut butter likes to settle. A hard boil drives the peanut oil straight back out of the emulsion and leaves you with a grainy, greasy sauce, so keep it at a lazy blip — a bubble breaking the surface every second or two. In that time it will thicken noticeably and stop tasting like separate ingredients sitting in a pan. If it thickens in much less than 3 minutes your burner is too high, so slide the pan half off the heat.

instructions.title: Thin to the right texture
instructions.text: Whisk in warm water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until it reaches the consistency you want — pourable like heavy cream for tossing with noodles, thicker like a loose hummus for dipping satay. It will thicken considerably as it cools, so leave it a little looser than seems right. Expect to use ¼ to ½ cup of water in total.

instructions.title: Finish with lime off the heat
instructions.text: Take the pan off the burner and stir in the 2 tbsp fresh lime juice. Lime juice added while the sauce is still cooking loses its perfume and goes slightly bitter, so it always goes in at the end. Taste now: it should hit salty, sweet, and sour in quick succession with warmth from the curry paste behind it.

instructions.title: Adjust and serve
instructions.text: Correct the balance with what it needs — 1 tsp more fish sauce for salt, 1 tsp more sugar for sweetness, another squeeze of lime for brightness, or a pinch of chile flakes for heat. Pour it into a bowl and scatter the chopped roasted peanuts over the top for crunch. Serve warm or at room temperature with chicken satay, summer rolls, grilled pork, or cold noodles.

tips: It thickens a lot in the fridge. Reheat gently with a splash of water or coconut milk, stirring, and it comes right back.
Keeps 1 week refrigerated at or below 40°F (4°C) and freezes for 3 months. Make a double batch — it disappears fast.
For a peanut allergy, swap in the same amount of sunflower seed butter or tahini. Tahini makes a noticeably more savory, less sweet sauce.
Thinned with an extra ¼ cup (60 ml) of water and an extra tablespoon of lime, this becomes an excellent dressing for a crunchy cabbage and carrot salad.
Curry pastes vary hugely in heat. Start with 1 tbsp if you are unsure, taste after the sauce comes together, and add more from there.
recipes.keyTemp: No internal temperature applies. Keep the pan at a gentle simmer near 190°F (88°C) — a hard boil splits the peanut oil out and turns the sauce grainy. Chicken satay served alongside must reach 165°F (74°C), and grilled pork 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest.
recipes.pairing: Chicken satay, fresh summer rolls, or cold rice noodles; a cold Singha or a slightly sweet Riesling handles the heat.

recipes.title: All-Purpose Steak and Beef Rub
recipes.blurb: Whole peppercorns and coriander toasted and cracked with salt, garlic, and paprika into a rub that makes any cut of beef taste like it was cooked by someone who knows what they are doing.
recipes.servings: Makes about 1¼ cups (165 g), enough for 8 to 10 steaks

items: ¼ cup (36 g) whole black peppercorns
2 tbsp (12 g) whole coriander seeds
1 tbsp (6 g) whole cumin seeds, optional
⅓ cup (45 g) coarse kosher salt (Diamond Crystal), or 3 tbsp (45 g) Morton kosher salt
2 tbsp (16 g) garlic powder
1 tbsp (8 g) onion powder
1 tbsp (7 g) sweet or smoked paprika
2 tsp (2 g) dried thyme
2 tsp (5 g) mustard powder
1 tsp (2 g) cayenne pepper
2 tbsp (26 g) packed dark brown sugar, optional and only for grilling

instructions.title: Start with whole spices
instructions.text: Pre-ground pepper loses most of its aromatic oils within a few weeks of grinding, which is why a jar of black pepper from the back of the cupboard tastes like dust. Whole peppercorns and coriander seeds toasted and cracked fresh are a genuinely different ingredient. This one change does more for the rub than any other.

instructions.title: Toast them dry
instructions.text: Put the peppercorns, coriander seeds, and cumin seeds if using in a dry skillet over medium heat and toast for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking the pan constantly. They are ready when the coriander turns a shade darker and the mixture smells warm and citrusy — you may hear a few seeds pop. Tip them onto a cold plate right away, because a hot pan keeps toasting them into bitterness.

instructions.title: Cool before grinding
instructions.text: Let the toasted spices cool completely, about 5 minutes. Warm spices are oily and will gum up a grinder or clump into a paste instead of cracking cleanly. Cooling also lets the flavors set; freshly toasted spices smell fantastic but taste flatter than they will in ten minutes.

instructions.title: Crack, do not pulverize
instructions.text: Pulse the cooled spices in a clean coffee grinder 5 or 6 times, or crush them in a mortar or under the bottom of a heavy pan. You want a coarse crack with pieces roughly the size of coarse sand, not a fine powder. Coarse cracked pepper forms a crust on a steak that you can actually see and feel; powder just dissolves and can burn.

instructions.title: Combine with the dry seasonings
instructions.text: Tip the cracked spices into a bowl with the kosher salt, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, dried thyme, mustard powder, and cayenne. Whisk for a full 30 seconds so it is completely uniform — powders love to settle in layers. Crush the dried thyme between your palms as you add it to release its oils.

instructions.title: Decide about the sugar
instructions.text: Add the 2 tbsp brown sugar only if you are grilling or smoking, where it caramelizes into a beautiful crust over indirect heat. Leave it out for high-heat searing in a cast iron pan, because sugar starts to burn around 350°F (177°C) and a sear runs far hotter than that. Keeping two jars, one sweet and one not, is worth the five extra minutes.

instructions.title: Know the salt ratio
instructions.text: This rub is a little over a quarter salt by weight — about 45 g of salt in a 165 g batch — which means roughly 1½ tbsp of rub per pound (450 g) of meat lands you near the 0.7 percent salt that seasons beef properly. If you are salting a steak separately, use a version of this blend with the salt left out so you do not double up. Measuring by the meat's weight rather than by eye is the fastest way to stop under- or over-seasoning.

instructions.title: Apply it properly
instructions.text: Pat the steaks completely dry with paper towels, then sprinkle the rub from about 10 inches (25 cm) above so it falls evenly instead of landing in clumps. Press it in gently with your palm — do not rub aggressively, which just drags the seasoning into piles. Cover every surface including the fat cap and the edges.

instructions.title: Let it dry brine
instructions.text: Set the seasoned steaks on a rack over a sheet pan and refrigerate uncovered for at least 45 minutes, or up to 24 hours for thick cuts. The salt first pulls moisture to the surface, then that seasoned liquid is reabsorbed while the exterior dries out, which is precisely what you need for a hard sear. A steak seasoned and cooked immediately steams instead of browning.

instructions.title: Store it in the dark
instructions.text: Keep the rub in an airtight jar somewhere cool and dark, away from the stove where heat and steam degrade spices fastest. It stays vibrant for about 3 months and remains safe far longer, just gradually duller. Write the date on the lid, because everyone thinks they will remember and nobody does.

tips: This is excellent on more than steak — try it on burgers, on a pork shoulder before a long roast, on roasted potatoes, and on thick-cut mushrooms.

Salt brands are not interchangeable by volume. Morton kosher salt is nearly twice as dense as Diamond Crystal, so use about 3 tbsp of Morton where this recipe calls for ⅓ cup of Diamond Crystal — or simply weigh out 45 g of whichever one you own.
For a Montreal-style version, double the coriander and add 1 tbsp (5 g) dried dill seed.
Make a salt-free version of the same blend and keep it beside the salted one. It lets you season meat by weight with salt first and add flavor separately, which is how restaurants do it.
recipes.keyTemp: The rub has no cooking temperature of its own. Use it on steaks and pull them off the heat early, because carryover keeps cooking them: 125°F (52°C) pull rests up to about 130°F to 135°F (54°C to 57°C) for medium-rare, and a 135°F (57°C) pull rests up to about 140°F to 145°F (60°C to 63°C) for medium. Ground beef gets no such latitude and must be cooked through to 160°F (71°C).
recipes.pairing: Built for ribeyes and strip steaks off a screaming cast iron pan or a hot grill, with a bold Cabernet.

recipes.title: Pan Gravy from Roast Drippings
recipes.blurb: The gravy you make in the roasting pan while the bird rests, built on flour, fat, and everything stuck to the bottom. Nothing from a jar has ever come close.

items: 6 tbsp (90 ml) fat skimmed from the roasting pan drippings, topped up with butter if short
6 tbsp (45 g) all-purpose flour
3 cups (700 ml) hot stock — turkey, chicken, or beef — plus the defatted pan juices
½ cup (120 ml) dry white wine or dry sherry, for deglazing
1 sprig fresh thyme and 1 fresh sage leaf
1 tsp (5 ml) soy sauce, optional, for color and savory depth
½ tsp (3 g) kosher salt, plus more to taste
½ tsp (1 g) freshly ground black pepper
1 tsp (5 ml) fresh lemon juice or cider vinegar, to finish
1 tbsp (14 g) cold unsalted butter, optional, for gloss
1 tsp (3 g) cornstarch whisked into 1 tbsp (15 ml) cold water, in reserve, only if the gravy needs more body

instructions.title: Move the roast and rest it
instructions.text: Lift the finished roast onto a board or platter and let it rest, loosely tented, while you make the gravy — 20 minutes for a chicken, 30 to 45 for a turkey. Confirm it hit its safe temperature before you start using the juices: 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part of a turkey or chicken thigh, 145°F (63°C) plus a 3-minute rest for pork. The rest and the gravy take almost exactly the same amount of time, which is not a coincidence.

instructions.title: Separate the fat
instructions.text: Pour everything in the roasting pan into a fat separator or a tall glass measuring cup and let it settle for 5 minutes. The clear fat rises to the top and the dark savory juices sink below it. Skim off 6 tbsp (90 ml) of the fat for your roux and save the juices — those juices are pure concentrated flavor and go into the gravy later.

instructions.title: Deglaze the roasting pan
instructions.text: Set the roasting pan across two burners over medium heat, pour in the ½ cup wine, and scrape hard with a flat wooden spatula. Every stuck brown patch should dissolve within about a minute of bubbling — that is the roasted flavor moving into your gravy. Let the wine keep bubbling until it has reduced by about half, another 2 minutes, so the finished gravy tastes of roast rather than raw alcohol. Pour this liquid in with the reserved pan juices and set it aside.

instructions.title: Start the roux
instructions.text: Put the 6 tbsp reserved fat in a 3-quart (3 L) saucepan over medium heat. If you came up short on fat, top it up with butter — you need the full 6 tbsp to match the flour, because a roux is equal parts fat and flour by volume, and 6 tbsp of each is what it takes to thicken 3 to 4 cups of liquid into gravy rather than soup. Wait until the fat shimmers before the flour goes in.

instructions.title: Cook the flour out
instructions.text: Whisk in the 6 tbsp flour all at once and cook, whisking constantly, for 2 to 3 minutes. The paste will foam, then smooth out, then start smelling nutty like toast rather than raw and pasty. For a darker, deeper gravy suited to beef, keep going another 2 minutes until it is the color of peanut butter, but watch it closely because roux burns quickly.

instructions.title: Add liquid gradually
instructions.text: Have your stock and pan juices hot, then add them to the roux about ½ cup (120 ml) at a time, whisking each addition until completely smooth before the next goes in. Adding hot liquid to hot roux slowly is the whole secret to lump-free gravy — dump it all in cold and the flour seizes into knots instantly. It will look alarmingly thick after the first addition; that is correct.

instructions.title: Simmer and thicken
instructions.text: Once all the liquid is in, add the thyme sprig and sage leaf and bring the gravy to a full simmer at about 200°F (93°C), whisking often. Let it bubble for 5 to 8 minutes; flour-thickened sauces do not reach their full thickening power until they actually boil. It will thicken visibly during this time.

instructions.title: Adjust the consistency
instructions.text: The gravy should coat the back of a spoon so that a finger drawn across leaves a clear path. If it is too thin, simmer a few more minutes or whisk in a slurry of 1 tsp cornstarch mixed with 1 tbsp (15 ml) cold water. If it is too thick, whisk in hot stock 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time — remember it thickens further as it cools on the plate.

instructions.title: Fix any lumps
instructions.text: Lumps are not a disaster and they are never a reason to start over. Pour the gravy through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean pan, pressing the lumps against the mesh with the back of a ladle, or run a stick blender through it for about 10 seconds until it is smooth. Do this before you season, because straining always leaves a little volume behind in the sieve and you want to be salting the exact amount of gravy you will actually serve. Wipe out the first pan and pour the gravy back in if it is the only warm pan you have.

instructions.title: Season carefully
instructions.text: Pull out the herbs, then taste and add the ½ tsp salt and ½ tsp pepper. Go slowly on salt: pan drippings from a brined or heavily seasoned bird can already be very salty, and you cannot take it out. Add the 1 tsp soy sauce if the gravy looks pale or tastes thin — it deepens both color and savoriness without reading as soy.

instructions.title: Brighten and gloss it
instructions.text: Off the heat, stir in the 1 tsp lemon juice or cider vinegar and, if you like, whisk in the cold tablespoon of butter until it disappears. The acid cuts through all that fat and makes the gravy taste less heavy, while the butter gives it a glossy sheen. Both take ten seconds and both are genuinely worth doing.

instructions.title: Hold it hot and serve
instructions.text: Keep the gravy above 140°F (60°C) until serving, either over the lowest burner setting or in a warmed gravy boat, and whisk it if a skin forms. Any juices that pool under the resting roast go in at the last second. Leftover gravy keeps 3 days refrigerated below 40°F (4°C) and reheats well with a splash of stock.

tips: Make a backup batch of gravy ahead of time using stock and butter instead of drippings, then whisk the real drippings into it at the last minute. It removes every bit of holiday panic.
Roast a few chicken wings, an onion, and a carrot alongside the bird if you are worried about not having enough drippings. They render plenty of flavorful fat and fond.
For gluten-free gravy, skip the roux entirely and thicken 3 cups of the deglazed liquid with a slurry of 3 tbsp (24 g) cornstarch in ¼ cup (60 ml) cold water, simmered 2 minutes.
Giblet gravy: simmer the neck and giblets in the stock for 45 minutes while the bird roasts, then chop the meat fine and stir it in at the end.
Always heat the stock before adding it. Cold liquid into hot roux is the single most common cause of lumpy gravy.
recipes.keyTemp: The roast itself must reach 165°F (74°C) in the thigh for poultry before its juices go into the gravy. Bring the finished gravy to a full simmer at 200°F (93°C) and hold it above 140°F (60°C) until served.
recipes.pairing: Poured over roast turkey or chicken with mashed potatoes and stuffing; a light Pinot Noir or a hard cider works with either.
